sections.title: Mental model — continuous worlds & counting functions

blocks.md: **Two upgrades this level: answers become REAL numbers (precision discipline), and feasibility becomes a COUNTING function over huge virtual spaces.**

blocks.label: bulletproof real-BS pattern
blocks.py:
lo, hi = 0.0, 1e18
for _ in range(100):                     # fixed iterations beat eps loops
    mid = (lo + hi) / 2
    if feasible(mid): hi = mid
    else:             lo = mid
# answer ~ hi; 100 halvings crush any double precision need

blocks.md: **Never `while (hi−lo > eps)` on adversarial doubles** — rounding stalls. Fixed iterations always terminate; say '100 iterations ≪ time limit' and move on.

items.q: Feasible(mid)=true with minimize-goal moves which bound?
options: hi=mid — true region keeps shrinking toward optimum

blocks.md: Binary predicate dead? If f is UNIMODAL (rises then falls), compare two interior probes m1<m2: f(m1)<f(m2) ⇒ peak right of m1; else peak left of m2. Discard a THIRD each round — Θ(log₁·₅ n).

blocks.title: Trace: ternary max of f=[0,2,5,9,7,3,1] (peak at index 3)

items: Integer ternary needs careful mid placement (m1=lo+(hi-lo)/3, m2=hi-(hi-lo)/3) + plateau warnings
Alternative for integer unimodal: binary-search slope sign (a[mid]<a[mid+1]) — usually cleaner (peak template L2)
Real unimodal optimization (geometry/physics) = ternary's home turf

items.q: Value-bisect vs heap-merge decision hinges on…
options: k's magnitude — bisect cost independent of k
items.explain: k near n² favors bisection massively.

blocks.md: Matrix sorted rows+cols, multiplication tables, pair-distances — all share one skeleton: **guess VALUE v → count elements ≤ v in O(n) or O(n+m) via structure → monotone count(v) → bisect v.** You never enumerate the giant implicit universe.

blocks.label: sorted-matrix counter (staircase count ≤ x)
blocks.py:
cnt, r, c = 0, 0, m - 1
while r < n and c >= 0:                  # start top-right
    if mat[r][c] <= x:
        cnt += c + 1                     # whole prefix of row counted
        r += 1
    else:
        c -= 1

chain.a: Sort once; count pairs ≤ d via sliding window j-pointer per i — Θ(n) per guess; total Θ(n log(maxDist)). Same doctrine as LC378 but linear-space counting.

chain.q: Why not heap-merge k smallest instead?
chain.a: Heap gives k extractions × log k each — fine for small k, dies at k~n²/4 midpoints. Value-bisect independent of k's magnitude — that's the CP-grade distinction.
Same 'jump powers of two' DNA as exponential search & sparse-table level selection; full treatment arrives with trees/LCA module.

options: NON-DECREASING — ties handled by first-true hunting

items.title: Kth Smallest Element in Sorted Matrix
items.statement: Full pipeline: counter above + value bisection; report complexity Θ((n+m)·log(range)).

solutionCode.label: bisect the VALUE, count with the staircase walk

items.complexity: Theta((n + m) * log(range)) — a staircase count per guess, over the value range. Space O(1). Beats the O(n^2 log n) heap-free sort and the O(k log n) heap when k is large.

followups.q: Why is the answer guaranteed to be an actual matrix entry?
followups.a: The search converges to the smallest x with count(x) >= k. If x were not in the matrix, then count(x) == count(x-1), so x-1 would also satisfy the predicate and x would not be the smallest. The predicate can only turn true at a value that is present.

followups.q: Why bisect the value rather than the position?
followups.a: There is no global position ordering — the matrix is sorted by row and by column, but not row-major overall, so index k has no meaning. Values, however, are totally ordered and countable in O(n+m). When positions are not searchable, search the value space instead.

items.title: Kth Smallest Number in Multiplication Table
items.statement: Table never materialized. Per-guess Σ min(x/i, m).
hints: Loop rows only up to min(n, x).

solutionCode.label: count row by row without materialising the table

items.complexity: O(n log(n*m)) — one O(n) count per guess. The table is never built, which is the point: n*m can reach 9*10^10 cells.

followups.q: Why min(m, x/i) rather than just x/i?
followups.a: Row i contains i*1 through i*m, so j never exceeds m. Without the cap, a small i would claim x/i columns that do not exist — for i = 1 and x large that overcounts the entire row. The cap is what keeps the count tied to the real table.

n and m reach 3*10^4, so n*m is about 9*10^8 — the hi bound alone is near the 32-bit ceiling, and the running count sums up to that. Overflow here silently produces a negative count, which makes the predicate lie and the search return garbage.

items.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Array II + Infinite Mountain (combo drill)
items.statement: Mountain array behind unknown-length interface: exponential-grow bounds until slope flips, then peak-hunt.
hints: Then reuse L2 converging peak loop.

solutionCode.label: exponentially grow the window, then run the L2 peak hunt

items.complexity: O(log P) probes to bracket the peak plus O(log P) to find it, where P is the peak index. The array length is unknown, so bounds must be discovered.

followups.q: Why doubling rather than a linear walk?
followups.a: A linear walk to find the end costs O(P) probes, which defeats the point of a logarithmic search. Doubling reaches or passes the peak in log(P) probes, and the bracket [hi/2, hi] is guaranteed to contain it because hi/2 was still ascending and hi was not. Total stays O(log P).

followups.q: Why treat out-of-range as +infinity here rather than -infinity?
followups.a: Careful: it must behave as a *descent* signal so the search turns back. Returning +infinity in `val` and then testing `b == INF or a > b` forces the hi = mid branch, which shrinks toward the real data. Returning a genuinely large value instead would make the search walk off the end chasing a phantom climb.

items.title: Smallest Divisor Given Threshold
items.statement: Min divisor d so Σ ceil(a[i]/d) ≤ threshold — decreasing checker.

solutionCode.label: the same ceil-sum checker as Koko, different noun

followups.a: With d = max(a) every ceil(x/d) is 1, so the sum equals n. The problem guarantees threshold >= n, so that divisor is always feasible and nothing larger can help. Setting hi higher only wastes iterations; setting it lower risks excluding the answer.

followups.q: How is this the same problem as Koko?
followups.a: Identical: sum of ceil(a[i]/d) must stay under a budget, and the sum is non-increasing in d. Piles become numbers, eating speed becomes the divisor, hours become the threshold. Recognising it saves you from re-deriving the monotonicity argument under time pressure.

items.title: Real-Valued Split Min-Max (continuous books)
items.statement: Segment [0,L] line into k pieces minimizing longest piece where cut cost curve given — solve with 100-iteration real BS; explain why ints fail.

solutionCode.label: fixed-iteration real binary search: never loop on lo < hi with doubles

items.complexity: O(n * iterations) with iterations fixed at 100 — roughly 2^-100 relative precision, far beyond double resolution. Space O(1).

followups.a: The optimal cut length need not be an integer — segments can be real-valued, so the answer lives between integers. Rounding the search to integers can only overshoot or undershoot, and the error does not shrink with more iterations. The search space itself is continuous.

followups.q: Why a fixed iteration count instead of looping while hi - lo > eps?
followups.a: With doubles, hi - lo can stagnate above your epsilon once you hit the limits of floating-point resolution, and the loop never terminates. 100 halvings shrink the interval by 2^-100, which is below double precision for any realistic range — it is guaranteed to finish and guaranteed to be exact to the last representable bit.

items.title: Ternary Terrain Peak
items.statement: Given strictly unimodal f as black-box array of size 10⁶, locate argmax via ternary; then re-solve with slope-bisect and compare probe counts.
hints: Slope version usually fewer probes — quantify.

solutionCode.label: ternary search, and the cheaper slope-bisect for comparison

items.complexity: Ternary: about 2*log_{1.5}(n) ~ 2*log(n)/log(1.5) probes. Slope-bisect: about log2(n) probes. For n = 10^6 that is roughly 68 versus 20 — the slope version wins by ~3x.

followups.a: Ternary discards one third per round, so the range shrinks by 2/3 and it needs log(n)/log(1.5) rounds at TWO probes each — about 68 probes for n = 10^6. Slope-bisect halves the range at two probes per round, log2(10^6) ~ 20 rounds, roughly 40 probes; with caching of f[mid] it is closer to 20. Ternary is the more general tool, not the faster one.

followups.q: When must you use ternary rather than slope-bisect?
followups.a: When f is a continuous real function where "the next point" does not exist, so you cannot compare f[mid] with f[mid+1]. On a discrete array the neighbour always exists, which is exactly what makes the cheaper slope test available. Reaching for ternary on an array is a habit worth un-learning.

revisionCard: Real BS: 100 fixed iterations > eps loops; announce precision math
Ternary = unimodal-only; strictness mandatory; slope-bisect often cleaner
Value-space doctrine: guess v → structural count(v) → bisect; never materialize universe
Staircase counter kills a row-or-column chunk per step
Exponential search brackets unbounded domains before bisection
Complexity formula: counterCost × log(range) — state it every time
Plateau safety: non-decreasing counts OK via first-true semantics
